cards.q: What does it mean for a system to be scalable?
cards.a: It can handle more users, data and requests just by adding resources, without being rebuilt. Test: if traffic doubles, can I just add machines, or must I change the design?

cards.q: What is vertical scaling, and why is it attractive?
cards.a: **Scaling up**: making one machine stronger with more CPU, more memory (RAM) or a faster disk. It is very simple: no code changes, and all data stays in one place.

cards.q: What are the downsides of vertical scaling?
cards.a: There is a ceiling (the biggest machine you can buy), you pay for the peak all day, it is a single point of failure, and an upgrade often needs a restart.

cards.q: What are the good sides of horizontal scaling?
cards.a: Almost no ceiling, it survives a machine dying, it uses many cheap normal machines, and the cloud can auto-scale: add machines when traffic goes up, remove them when it goes down.

cards.q: What makes horizontal scaling harder than vertical scaling?
cards.a: More moving parts to watch, servers must not keep user data in their own memory (they must be **stateless**), and spreading one database across many machines is hard.

cards.q: What is the usual order of steps as a system grows?
cards.a: One server → database on its own machine → more app servers behind a load balancer → cache and read replicas → queues, then shard → CDN and more regions.

cards.q: What is the difference between availability and reliability?
cards.a: **Availability**: is the system up when I need it? **Reliability**: does it work correctly, every time, over a long period? An ATM that is on but sometimes gives the wrong cash is available, not reliable.

cards.q: How much downtime per year do 99.9%, 99.99% and 99.999% uptime allow?
cards.a: Each extra nine means 10 times less downtime. 99.9%: about 8.8 hours (say 9). 99.99%: about 53 minutes. 99.999%: about 5.3 minutes.

cards.q: What happens to availability when parts are in a chain?
cards.a: It goes down, because all parts must work, so you multiply. A load balancer, app server and database at 99.9% each give about 99.7%.

cards.q: What happens to availability when two servers run side by side?
cards.a: It goes up, because the system is down only if both are down. Two servers at 99.9% are both down 0.001 × 0.001 of the time, so the pair is up 99.9999%.

cards.q: What is a single point of failure, and how do you find one?
cards.a: Any one part that takes the whole system down when it breaks. Point at each box and ask, "What happens if this one dies?" If everything stops, it is a SPOF.

cards.q: What techniques make a system more available?
cards.a: Redundancy (spare copies), failover (switch to the spare automatically), health checks, replication, many zones, graceful degradation and careful deploys.

cards.q: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
cards.a: **Latency** is how long one request takes. **Throughput** is how many requests the system can finish every second.

cards.q: How can you lower latency?
cards.a: Put data closer to users (CDN, more regions), cache popular data in memory, make fewer round trips, speed up queries with indexes, and do slow work later with a queue.

cards.q: Why should you design for the peak, not the average?
cards.a: Traffic is not flat: people use apps more in the evening, during a sale or during a big match. The peak is often 2 to 3 times the average, and much more during special events.

cards.q: Why can the average latency hide a problem?
cards.a: If 980 of 1,000 requests take 50 ms and 20 take 3 seconds, the average is 109 ms, which looks fine. But p99 is 3,000 ms: 2 users in every 100 wait 3 seconds. So use p50 and p99.

cards.q: How do batching, caching and queues affect latency and throughput?
cards.a: **Batching** raises throughput but adds latency, like a bus that waits until it is full. **Caching** improves both. **Queues** give the user a fast answer and do the slow work later.

cards.q: A request waits for 100 servers, and each is slow 1 time in 100. How often is the user's request slow?
cards.a: All 100 are fast only 0.99 to the power 100 ≈ 37% of the time, so about **63%** of user requests are slow. Rare slowness on each server becomes common slowness for users.

cards.q: What are arrival rate, service time and utilization?
cards.a: **Arrival rate:** how many requests come in per second. **Service time:** how long one takes to handle, not counting the wait. **Utilization:** how busy the server is = arrival rate ÷ service rate. 80 per second at 10 ms each = 80%.

cards.q: In the simple M/M/1 model, what is the average wait in the queue?
cards.a: **utilization ÷ (1 − utilization) × service time.** 50% busy → about 1× the service time, 80% → 4×, 90% → 9×, 99% → 99×. It is a simplified model, but real systems show the same shape: flat, then a steep wall near 100%.

cards.q: An API gets 1,000 requests per second, and each takes 0.2 s. How many are in flight?
cards.a: Little's Law: 1,000 × 0.2 = **200 requests in flight** (started, not finished). With one thread per request, you need at least 200 threads across all servers, and more for the peak.

cards.q: What happens to requests in flight when a dependency gets slow?
cards.a: They grow, even with the same traffic. At 1,000 per second, going from 0.2 s to 1 s per request means 1,000 in flight instead of 200. Threads and connection pools run out, and one slow database can freeze many app servers.

cards.q: When is it fine to run a server near 100% busy?
cards.a: For background or batch work, where nobody waits for each item: throughput matters, not latency. Latency-sensitive servers need headroom (a common rule of thumb: around 50 to 70% busy at peak), because waiting explodes near 100%.

cards.q: What practical rules keep queues from hurting latency?
cards.a: Leave headroom. Give every queue a size limit. Use timeouts, and drop requests that already waited longer than the caller will wait. When full, shed load (fast 503s) or push back on the sender. Watch queue length and wait time.

cards.q: What is the difference between a stateful and a stateless server?
cards.a: A **stateful** server keeps the knowledge in its own memory, so only it can serve that user. A **stateless** server keeps nothing between requests: the request carries it, or it is read from a shared store.

cards.q: Why do stateless servers scale easily?
cards.a: Any server can handle any request. Adding a server is easy, a crash loses nothing, and deploys just replace servers one at a time.

cards.q: Where should state live instead of in the app servers?
cards.a: Sessions in Redis or a signed token (JWT), carts in Redis or the database, users and orders in the database, files in object storage like S3, and waiting work in a queue.

cards.q: Which parts of a system must be stateful?
cards.a: Databases and caches, live connections like WebSockets, multiplayer game servers, and live document editing.

cards.q: What are sticky sessions?
cards.a: A load balancer setting (also called **session affinity**) that sends all of one user's requests to the same server, usually by setting a cookie.

cards.q: What are the downsides of sticky sessions?
cards.a: Uneven load, users still lose their sessions if the server dies, and it is harder to remove servers and deploy.

cards.q: What are the main jobs of a load balancer?
cards.a: Spread the load, skip dead servers, give one address for many servers, and extras like TLS termination (decrypting HTTPS once, so the servers don't have to) and routing by URL.

cards.q: How does least connections work, and when is it better than round robin?
cards.a: It sends each new request to the server with the fewest open requests right now. It is better when requests take very different times, and for long-lived connections like WebSockets.

cards.q: When would a load balancer pick the server by hashing a key?
cards.a: When the same user or key must reach the same server, because that server keeps something for it: a cache, a chat room, a game match. Use consistent hashing, so adding a server moves only a few keys.

cards.q: What is the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer?
cards.a: **L4** sees only IP addresses and ports, so it is very fast. **L7** reads the whole HTTP request (URL, headers, cookies), so it can route by path, host name, header or cookie.

cards.q: What does it mean to drain a server?
cards.a: Before removing a server on purpose, like during a deploy, the load balancer stops sending it new requests but lets requests in progress finish. AWS calls this the deregistration delay.

cards.q: How do you stop the load balancer from being a single point of failure?
cards.a: Never run just one. Use an active-passive pair with a floating IP, an active-active pair, or a managed cloud load balancer, which already runs on many machines across zones.

cards.q: How does a typical health check work?
cards.a: The load balancer calls an address like `GET /health` every few seconds. A `200 OK` answer means healthy. An error, or no answer in time, means not.

cards.q: Why not remove a server after one failed health check?
cards.a: Networks have small hiccups. Servers would keep dropping out and coming back. This is called **flapping**.

cards.q: What should the health check that decides traffic test, and why?
cards.a: Only what the server itself owns. If it tests the shared database and the database gets slow, every server fails at once, all are removed, and the whole site goes down.

cards.q: What is service discovery, and why is it needed?
cards.a: Finding a service's current addresses by its **name**. Servers come and go and their IPs change, so an IP like `10.0.3.17` written in a config file breaks when that server is replaced.

cards.q: What is the difference between client-side and server-side discovery?
cards.a: **Client-side**: the caller asks the registry and picks a server itself (Netflix Eureka). **Server-side**: the caller sends to one fixed address, like a load balancer, which looks up the registry (Kubernetes Services).

cards.q: What is the difference between a liveness and a readiness probe in Kubernetes?
cards.a: **Liveness**: is the app stuck? If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container. **Readiness**: can it take traffic? If it fails, the pod is taken out of the Service, but not restarted.

cards.q: What is an API gateway?
cards.a: One front door for all your backend services. Every request from outside comes to it first. It checks the request, then sends it to the right service.

cards.q: What are the main jobs of an API gateway?
cards.a: Routing, login checks (authentication), rate limiting, TLS termination, changing requests, combining answers, caching, logging and metrics, and versioning.

cards.q: Which check stays in the service, even with an API gateway?
cards.a: **Authorization**: "may user 42 cancel order 7?" Only the order service knows who owns order 7. The gateway only checks who you are (authentication).

cards.q: What is the difference between an API gateway and a load balancer?
cards.a: A **load balancer** spreads traffic across copies of the same service. A **gateway** sends requests to different services and applies API rules. A load balancer manages traffic; a gateway manages APIs.

cards.q: How should you run an API gateway safely?
cards.a: Run several copies behind a load balancer, so it is not a single point of failure. Keep it to routing and shared checks, or it becomes a small monolith that every team must change.

cards.q: When should you add an API gateway to a design?
cards.a: When there are several services, or a public API with keys and limits. With a single service, a load balancer is enough.

cards.q: What goes wrong with a monolith as it grows?
cards.a: Every change means deploying the whole app, teams get in each other's way, one bug can take everything down, you must scale everything together, and you are stuck with one tech stack.

cards.q: What are the downsides of microservices?
cards.a: Network calls are slower and can fail, there are no simple transactions across services (you need patterns like Saga), debugging needs tracing, and there is much more to run.

cards.q: When should you pick a monolith?
cards.a: When the product is new and still changing, the team is small, you don't yet know the clean lines between parts, and building fast matters most.

cards.q: When should you pick microservices?
cards.a: When many teams need to ship on their own, parts have very different load or need different tech, and you already have good automation: deploys, monitoring, tracing.

cards.q: What is a modular monolith?
cards.a: One app with one deploy, but the code is split into clear modules with strict rules about who may call whom. You can still pull a module out into its own service later.

cards.q: How should you move from a monolith to microservices?
cards.a: Piece by piece with the **strangler pattern**, never a big rewrite: put a gateway in front, move one part with clear edges to a new service with its own data, send its traffic there, repeat.

cards.q: What are the handy shortcuts for multiplying counts by sizes?
cards.a: A million × 1 KB = 1 GB. A billion × 1 KB = 1 TB. A million × 1 MB = 1 TB.

cards.q: How long do a memory read, an SSD random read and a round trip inside one data center take?
cards.a: Memory (RAM): 100 ns. Random read from an SSD: 100 µs (0.1 ms). Round trip inside one data center: 0.5 ms.

cards.q: How long is a network round trip across an ocean, and what does that teach you?
cards.a: USA East Coast ↔ Europe: about 80 ms. India ↔ USA: about 200 ms. Across an ocean is expensive, so put data near users and avoid many round trips.

cards.q: How do you get average and peak QPS from daily active users (DAU)?
cards.a: Requests per day = DAU × actions per user per day. Average QPS = requests per day ÷ 100,000. Peak QPS ≈ average × 2 or 3 (more for very spiky apps, like ticket sales).

cards.q: Chat app: 50 million daily users send 40 messages each. What write QPS, and what follows?
cards.a: 2 billion a day ÷ 100,000 ≈ 20,000 per second, about 60,000 at peak. Far too many for one SQL primary: shard by chat ID, or use a write-friendly database like Cassandra.

cards.q: What should every capacity number lead to?
cards.a: A design decision: cache, shard, S3 or CDN. Ask: Does the data fit on one machine? Can one database take the writes? Is it read-heavy? Is the bandwidth huge?

cards.q: Why do reads usually become the first database problem?
cards.a: Most apps are **read-heavy**: reads can be 100 times more than writes, or more. One database machine can only answer so many reads per second.

cards.q: In what order should you try fixes for a read-heavy system?
cards.a: Index → cache → read replicas → CDN → precompute. Try them in order; don't jump to the hard ones first.

cards.q: What is a read replica, and what is its catch?
cards.a: A copy of the database that only answers reads. The **primary** takes all writes and copies them over. Catch: a replica can be a little behind, so read a user's own new writes from the primary.

cards.q: What is precomputing?
cards.a: Preparing answers early. Instead of counting likes every time someone views a post, store the like count and update it when a like happens.

cards.q: Why should you say the read-to-write ratio early in an interview?
cards.a: It tells you the read-scaling pattern is needed. For example, "about 100 reads for every write" leads to a cache, read replicas and a CDN.

cards.q: Why don't read replicas help with writes?
cards.a: Every copy must store every write. With one primary, all writes go through it, and each replica must copy every write, which adds work. Only splitting the data across machines adds write capacity.

cards.q: Why is batching writes faster than writing rows one by one?
cards.a: Every write has a fixed cost: a network round trip, starting a transaction, and saving to disk. Writing 1,000 rows in one go is much cheaper than 1,000 separate writes.

cards.q: How does a queue help with write spikes?
cards.a: The app puts each write in a queue and answers "got it" right away. Workers write at a steady speed the database can handle. If the database is down for a minute, the writes wait in the queue.

cards.q: How does sharding scale writes?
cards.a: It splits the data across several databases, each with its own primary taking only its share of the writes: 10 shards take about 10 times the writes. Pick a shard key that spreads writes evenly.

cards.q: Why is `UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1` a problem for a viral post?
cards.a: Thousands of likes per second all update the same row. The database locks the row for each update, so they all wait in one line. This is a **hot row**.

cards.q: How can you count likes at scale?
cards.a: Count in Redis with `INCR` and have a job save the totals every few seconds, batch increments in each app server, use sharded counters, use a HyperLogLog for unique counts, or send events to Kafka for a counting job.
